description: We are computer science students at Tlajomulco Technological Institute (TecNM) in Jalisco, Mexico, and our areas of interest are: mobile computing, AI, and web development. We are excited to participate in this event, in order to create professional relationships with other groups, and share knowledge and friendship as well.
summary: TerraLens is a web app that answers one question for Los Altos de Jalisco, a semi-arid farming region of 20 municipalities in western Mexico: is the land drying out? It turns 44 years of NASA POWER data (MERRA-2, 1981–2024) on rainfall and soil moisture into answers anyone can read. On a 3D globe, you pick a zone or municipality and a period; the app compares each month with the 1991–2020 normal, measures meteorological drought (SPI) and soil water stress, and tests every trend twice: linear regression with autocorrelation-robust errors and Mann-Kendall. It tells you whether a change is clear, how large it is per decade, and, if it is not clear yet, how many more years of data would settle it. The NASA data is checked against 20 CONAGUA rain gauges (r = 0.96) and Mexico's Drought Monitor; an Outlook extends the trend to 2035 with its uncertainty, and Gemini writes a plain-language summary that may only use numbers the app already calculated. So far, rainfall shows no clear trend, soil moisture declines season by season, and drought keeps returning. We want farmers, students, and local officials to understand and plan for the water where they live.
details:
What it does

  • TerraLens covers the 20 municipalities of Los Altos de Jalisco, Mexico, a semi-arid highland region where farms and dairy cattle depend on seasonal rain. We chose it because it is drought-prone and water decides the harvest.
  • It tracks rainfall and soil moisture (surface, root zone, and full profile) and answers four questions for any zone (the whole region, Altos Norte or Altos Sur) and period: Is rainfall changing? Has there been meteorological drought? Is soil moisture changing? Has there been soil water stress? It also shows where change is strongest, how sure we can be, and what the next years could look like.
  • Each section shows the chart first, then a "What does it mean?" box, a "What it is not" note where needed, and its sources and limitations.
  • A 3D globe flies from the whole planet to Los Altos and paints each municipality with its own rainfall trend. Search or click a town to fly there.

How it works

  1. Data: monthly NASA POWER series (MERRA-2 model) for the 12 grid cells (about 50 km each) that cover the region. Each zone and municipality is the area-weighted average of the cells that cover it. The 1981–2024 series are stored with the app, so it also works offline.
  2. Normal: each month is compared with the same month in 1991–2020 (the World Meteorological Organization standard normal), which removes the seasonal cycle.
  3. Drought and stress: Standardized Precipitation Index, SPI-3 and SPI-6 (a gamma fit for each calendar month, McKee et al., 1993); drought means SPI of −1 or below. Soil water stress is the standardized anomaly of soil moisture for each month.
  4. Trends: linear regression with Newey-West (HAC) errors and a 95% confidence interval, and the Mann-Kendall test with Sen's slope, the Hamed-Rao correction and its seasonal form. A trend is called "clear" only when both tests agree (p < 0.05); otherwise, the app says how many more years of data would be needed.
  5. Outlook: annual values extended to 2030–2035 with a 95% prediction interval, and the chance of at least one drought year in the next 5 and 10 years if the past repeats, 1 − (1 − p)^n. It is a frequency, not a forecast.
  6. Checks on the ground: annual NASA POWER rainfall against 20 CONAGUA (SMN) rain gauges (Pearson correlation), and our SPI against Mexico's Drought Monitor (D0–D4 by municipality).
  7. Plain-language summary: Python builds a structured summary of the results, and Gemini explains it under strict rules: no new numbers, no causes, no crop advice. If its answer contains any number that is not in the results, it is discarded, and a template-based summary is shown instead.

What we found (2001–2024, whole region)

  • Rainfall: about 652 mm per year and no clear trend yet: −3.04 mm per month per decade (regression p = 0.249, Mann-Kendall p = 0.635). About 10 more years of data would settle it.
  • Meteorological drought: 36 of 288 months; the worst episode ran from January 2011 to January 2012 (extreme drought). 11 of 24 years had at least one drought month, so a drought year in the next five is about 95% likely if the past repeats.
  • Soil moisture (root zone): no clear overall trend, but the seasonal test detects a decline (p = 0.016). It is declining in Altos Sur (p = 0.001), not yet in Altos Norte (p = 0.051).
  • Soil water stress: 25 of 288 months, 10 of them in the last 5 years.
  • Checks: NASA POWER rainfall rises and falls with the CONAGUA rain gauges (r = 0.96 over 23 complete years), about 6% lower on average. Of the 34 months our SPI-6 marked as drought, 24 (71%) were also official drought.
  • These data show changes, not their causes.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Farmers, students, and local officials get evidence about their own region in plain language, with no coding or statistics needed.
  • Honest about uncertainty: "no clear trend" is a valid result, shown together with how many more years of data would settle it.
  • Guarded AI: the language model explains the numbers but cannot invent them.
  • Next steps: finer satellite products (GPM IMERG for rain, GLDAS and SMAP for soil moisture), more regions of Mexico and early drought warnings for producers.

What makes it creative

  • It interprets instead of only plotting: every result becomes a verdict, a size and a level of certainty, checked on the ground.
  • A 3D globe that goes from the whole planet to each municipality, painted by its own trend.
  • Two independent statistical tests plus a check against local rain gauges and an official drought monitor, in one app anyone can open.

Factors we considered

  • Uncertainty: two tests must agree, autocorrelation is corrected, and the Outlook is labeled as a frequency, not a forecast.
  • Scale: each NASA POWER cell covers about 50 km, so the app describes zones, not single plots.
  • Accessibility: English by default (Spanish for review), charts first and explanations below, readable contrast, and a lighter version on phones.
  • Responsible AI: no invented numbers, no causes, no crop advice; AI use is labeled in the app and in the demo video.

Tools, languages and software

Python 3.12, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, Plotly, requests and pytest; globe.gl and three.js for the 3D globe and relief; Git and GitHub. AI: the Gemini API (plain-language summary in the app and narration voice of the demo), Claude Code (coding assistant) and HyperFrames (demo video). Source code: https://github.com/FelipeCeervantes/earth-data-detectives

Limitations

  • NASA POWER cells cover about 50 km: the app describes zones, not individual plots or exact municipal values.
  • Soil moisture comes from a model (MERRA-2), not from field measurements, and the model uses rainfall as an input.
  • SPI measures meteorological drought only; soil water stress here means drier-than-normal soil, not proven crop stress.
  • The app shows changes and their statistical confidence, not their causes.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources): monthly rainfall and soil wetness, 1981–2024
MERRA-2 reanalysis (NASA GMAO), the model behind NASA POWER
Gelaro et al. (2017), The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2)
NASA Visible Earth, Blue Marble: texture of the 3D globe
NASA SRTM elevation, via AWS Terrain Tiles: 3D relief of Los Altos
projectRefs: CONAGUA, Servicio Meteorológico Nacional: monthly rainfall of 20 rain gauges in Los Altos (ground check)
CONAGUA, Servicio Meteorológico Nacional: Mexico's Drought Monitor, municipal categories since 2003 (official check)
INEGI, Marco Geoestadístico: municipal boundaries of Jalisco
McKee, Doesken & Kleist (1993), drought frequency and duration (Standardized Precipitation Index)
Sen (1968), Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau
Hamed & Rao (1998), A modified Mann-Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data
Newey & West (1987), heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix
Gemini API (Google): plain-language summary in the app and narration voice of the demo video
HyperFrames: editing of the demo video
